summary.text: For any odd prime divisor \(p\) of a composite \(n\), lifting the exponent at multiples of the order of \(2\bmod p\) gives enough \(p\)-adic valuation in the product to show \(p\mid a(n-1)\), forcing the impossible conclusion \(p\mid2\); if \(n=2^s\), instead \(v_2(a(n-1))=s-1\) while \(2^s\mid2^{n-2}\), again ruling out the divisibility. For prime \(p\), Wilson’s theorem converts the hypothesis and the product formula into \(\prod_{1\le k<p-1}(2^k-1)=1\pmod p\); hence the order of \(2\) cannot be smaller than \(p-1\), since its corresponding factor would vanish, so the order is exactly \(p-1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 B_m=2^{m-1}\prod_{k=1}^{m-1}(2^k-1)\qquad(m\ge 1).
\]
Thus the sequence in the statement is
\[
 a(m)=\frac{B_m}{m!}.
\]
We will first prove that this quotient is an integer and establish the valuation estimates that will be needed later.

For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(x\). If \(p\) is odd, let
\[
 d=d_p=\operatorname{ord}_p(2),
\]
the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\). Since \(2\not\equiv0\pmod p\), Fermat's theorem gives \(2^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p\). Consequently
\[
 d\mid p-1,
\]
so in particular \(1\le d\le p-1\), and \(p\nmid d\). By the definition of multiplicative order,
\[
 p\mid 2^k-1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d\mid k. \tag{1}
\]

We use the following valuation consequence of lifting the exponent. If \(d\mid k\), say \(k=dj\) with \(j\ge1\), then
\[
 v_p(2^k-1)=v_p(2^d-1)+v_p(j). \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, put \(x=2^d\). We have \(p\mid x-1\), \(p\nmid x\), and \(p\) is odd, so the standard lifting-the-exponent identity gives
\(v_p(x^j-1)=v_p(x-1)+v_p(j)\). Since \(p\nmid d\), we also have \(v_p(k)=v_p(j)\), although only the displayed form (2) will be needed. Moreover, (1) with \(k=d\) shows
\[
 v_p(2^d-1)\ge1. \tag{3}
\]

We now derive the basic lower bound for the valuations of the product. For any positive integer \(N\), set
\[
 M=\left\lfloor\frac{N-1}{d}\right\rfloor.
\]
The positive multiples of \(d\) that are less than \(N\) are exactly
\(d,2d,\ldots,Md\). All valuations are nonnegative, so retaining only these factors, and then applying (2) and (3), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{k=1}^{N-1}v_p(2^k-1)
 &\ge \sum_{j=1}^{M}v_p(2^{dj}-1)\\
 &=\sum_{j=1}^{M}\bigl(v_p(2^d-1)+v_p(j)\bigr)\\
 &\ge M+\sum_{j=1}^{M}v_p(j)\\
 &=M+v_p(M!).
\end{aligned} \tag{4}
\]
This is the main valuation estimate.

We also need an upper bound for factorial valuations. Legendre's digit-sum formula says that, for a prime \(p\),
\[
 (p-1)v_p(N!)=N-s_p(N), \tag{5}
\]
where \(s_p(N)\) is the sum of the base-\(p\) digits of \(N\). If \(N>0\), then \(s_p(N)\ge1\); hence
\[
 v_p(N!)\le \left\lfloor\frac{N-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{6}
\]
The same inequality is immediate for \(N=0\).

We can now justify that every \(a(m)\) is integral. For \(p=2\), every factor \(2^k-1\) is odd, so
\[
 v_2(B_m)=m-1.
\]
By (6), \(v_2(m!)\le m-1\). Now let \(p\) be odd and let \(d=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\). The power \(2^{m-1}\) contributes no factor of \(p\), and (4), with \(N=m\), gives
\[
 v_p(B_m)=\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}v_p(2^k-1)
 \ge \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{d}\right\rfloor.
\]
Because \(d\le p-1\), this is at least
\(\lfloor(m-1)/(p-1)\rfloor\), which by (6) is at least \(v_p(m!)\). Thus \(v_p(m!)\le v_p(B_m)\) for every prime \(p\), proving \(m!\mid B_m\). In particular, \(a(m)\) is a positive integer and
\[
 a(m)m!=B_m. \tag{7}
\]

We next prove the decisive lemma for composite integers.

**Lemma.** Suppose \(n>2\), and let \(p\) be an odd prime divisor of \(n\) with \(p<n\). Then
\[
 p\mid a(n-1).
\]

Write \(n=pt\). Since \(p<n\), we have \(t\ge2\). Put \(d=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and
\[
 M=\left\lfloor\frac{n-2}{d}\right\rfloor.
\]
We first show \(M\ge t\). Since \(d\le p-1\),
\[
 td\le t(p-1)=pt-t=n-t\le n-2,
\]
the last inequality following from \(t\ge2\). Therefore \(t\le\lfloor(n-2)/d\rfloor=M\).

Apply (7) with \(m=n-1\). Because \(p\) is odd, the initial power \(2^{n-2}\) in \(B_{n-1}\) contributes no \(p\)-factor, and hence
\[
 v_p(a(n-1))+v_p((n-1)!)
 =\sum_{k=1}^{n-2}v_p(2^k-1). \tag{8}
\]
By (4), the right side is at least
\[
 M+v_p(M!). \tag{9}
\]
Since \(M\ge t\), certainly \(M\ge t\) and \((t-1)!\mid M!\), so
\[
 M+v_p(M!)\ge t+v_p((t-1)!). \tag{10}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
 v_p((pt-1)!)=(t-1)+v_p((t-1)!). \tag{11}
\]
For completeness, (11) follows directly from the usual factorial valuation identities. Among the factors of \((pt)!\), extracting one factor \(p\) from each multiple \(p,2p,\ldots,tp\) gives
\[
 v_p((pt)!)=t+v_p(t!).
\]
But also
\[
 v_p((pt)!)=v_p((pt-1)!)+v_p(pt)
 =v_p((pt-1)!)+1+v_p(t),
\]
and \(v_p(t!)=v_p((t-1)!)+v_p(t)\). Comparing these formulas yields (11).

Combining (8), (9), (10), and (11), we obtain
\[
 v_p(a(n-1))+(t-1)+v_p((t-1)!)
 \ge t+v_p((t-1)!),
\]
so \(v_p(a(n-1))\ge1\). This proves the lemma.

We now show that no composite \(n>2\) can satisfy the divisibility in the conjecture. There are two cases.

First suppose that \(n\) has an odd prime divisor \(p\). Since \(n\) is composite, \(p<n\): equality would say that \(n=p\) is prime. The lemma therefore gives
\(p\mid a(n-1)\). If one also had
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}, \tag{12}
\]
then, because \(p\mid n\), it would follow that
\(p\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}\). Subtracting the divisibility \(p\mid a(n-1)\), we would obtain \(p\mid2^{n-2}\). Since \(p\) is prime, this forces \(p\mid2\), contrary to \(p\) being odd. Thus (12) is impossible in this case.

It remains to treat a composite \(n>2\) with no odd prime divisor. By unique factorization, such an \(n\) has the form
\[
 n=2^s.
\]
Since \(n>2\), we have \(s\ge2\). We compute the exact 2-adic valuation of \(a(n-1)\). From (7), noting again that every \(2^k-1\) is odd,
\[
 v_2(a(n-1))+v_2((n-1)!)=n-2. \tag{13}
\]
Legendre's formula at \(2\) says
\[
 v_2(r!)=r-s_2(r). \tag{14}
\]
Here \(r=n-1=2^s-1\). Its binary expansion consists of exactly \(s\) ones, so \(s_2(2^s-1)=s\). Consequently
\[
 v_2((n-1)!)=(n-1)-s. \tag{15}
\]
Substitution in (13) gives
\[
 v_2(a(n-1))=s-1. \tag{16}
\]
Thus \(2^s\nmid a(n-1)\).

On the other hand, \(2^s\mid2^{n-2}\). Indeed, for \(s\ge2\),
\[
 2^s\ge s+2,
\]
which follows immediately by induction starting from equality at \(s=2\); hence \(n-2=2^s-2\ge s\). Therefore, if \(2^s=n\) divided
\(a(n-1)+2^{n-2}\), subtracting the already divisible term \(2^{n-2}\) would imply \(2^s\mid a(n-1)\), contradicting (16). This disposes of the power-of-two case.

We have proved:
\[
 n>2\ \text{and}\ n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad n\ \text{is prime}. \tag{17}
\]

It remains to prove the primitive-root assertion. Let \(p>2\) be prime and suppose
\[
 p\mid a(p-1)+2^{p-2}. \tag{18}
\]
Reduce the identity (7), now with \(m=p-1\), modulo \(p\). It becomes
\[
 a(p-1)(p-1)!\equiv
 2^{p-2}\prod_{k=1}^{p-2}(2^k-1)\pmod p. \tag{19}
\]
Wilson's theorem gives
\[
 (p-1)!\equiv-1\pmod p, \tag{20}
\]
while (18) gives
\[
 a(p-1)\equiv-2^{p-2}\pmod p. \tag{21}
\]
Using (20) and (21) in (19), we find
\[
 2^{p-2}\equiv
 2^{p-2}\prod_{k=1}^{p-2}(2^k-1)\pmod p.
\]
The factor \(2^{p-2}\) is nonzero modulo \(p\), so it can be cancelled. Hence
\[
 \prod_{k=1}^{p-2}(2^k-1)\equiv1\pmod p. \tag{22}
\]

Let \(d=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\). As observed at the beginning, \(d\mid p-1\) and \(d\ge1\). If \(d\ne p-1\), then the divisibility \(d\mid p-1\) implies
\[
 1\le d<p-1,
\]
so \(d\) is one of the indices \(1,2,\ldots,p-2\) occurring in (22). But \(2^d\equiv1\pmod p\) by the definition of \(d\), so the factor \(2^d-1\) in that product is zero modulo \(p\). The whole product would then be congruent to \(0\), contradicting (22). Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_p(2)=p-1. \tag{23}
\]
For a prime \(p\), Euler's totient is \(\varphi(p)=p-1\). Thus (23) says precisely that \(2\) has multiplicative order \(\varphi(p)\) modulo \(p\), i.e. that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\).

Finally, given any integer \(n>2\) satisfying
\(n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}\), statement (17) shows that \(n\) is prime. Applying the preceding prime argument with \(p=n\) then shows that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\). Hence \(n\) is prime and \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\), as claimed.
